BASIS FOR OFFER PRICE
The Price Band and Offer Price will be determined by our Company, in consultation with the Book Running Lead Managers,
and on the basis of assessment of market demand for the Equity Shares offered through the Book Building Process and on the
basis of quantitative and qualitative factors as described below. The face value of the Equity Shares is ₹1 each and the Offer
Price is [●] times the face value at the lower end of the Price Band and [●] times the face value at the higher end of the Price
Band.
Bidders should read the below mentioned information along with “Risk Factors”, “Our Business”, “Restated Consolidated
Financial Information” and “Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations”
beginning on pages 24, 179, 267 and 357, respectively, to have an informed view before making an investment decision.
Qualitative Factors
We believe that some of the qualitative factors which form the basis for computing the Offer Price are as follows:
1. Market leader in India – a liquid market for all stakeholders
• We have been the largest stock exchange in India in terms of total turnover in cash market and total turnover in equity
derivatives (based on notional turnover for equity options) from Fiscal 20011 to Fiscal 2026, and have also been the
largest stock exchange in India in terms of total turnover in exchange-traded currency derivatives (based on notional
turnover for currency options) from Fiscal 20092 to Fiscal 2026, according to the Redseer Report.
• As of March 31, 2026, we supported 253.66 million registered investor accounts, 1,325 trading members, 129.09
million Unique Registered Investors and 2,978 Listed Entities with a Market Capitalisation of Listed Entities of
₹411.25 trillion.
• According to World Federation of Exchanges, compared to the leading listed stock exchange groups globally, we
were the largest multi-asset class exchange in terms of number of trades in cash equities and contracts traded in equity
derivatives in Fiscal 2026 with a global market share of 11.38% in number of trades in cash equities and 51.18% in
contracts traded in equity derivatives.
• As of Fiscal 2026, we maintain leading market share positions in India across key asset classes, with market share of
92.99% in cash market (based on total turnover), 99.79% in equity futures (based on total turnover), 74.71% in equity
options (based on premium turnover), 99.48% in exchange-traded currency futures (based on total turnover), 100.00%
for exchange-traded currency options (based on total premium turnover), according to the Redseer Report.
2. Well positioned to benefit from India's structural growth tailwinds which drive strong network effects for NSE
• In Fiscal 2026, Total Fund Mobilisation on NSE was ₹20.33 trillion with ₹1.78 trillion mobilised by fresh listings
and offer for sale across the Mainboard and SME board in primary markets, according to the Redseer Report.
• We have been among the top three exchange groups globally in terms of number of new listings through IPO from
Fiscal 2023 to Fiscal 2026, according to the Redseer Report.
• Over 30 years (March 1996 to March 2026), Nifty 50 has posted annualised returns of 10.98% in ₹ terms (7.32% in
US$ terms), and Nifty 500 has posted annualised returns of 11.94% in ₹ terms (8.26% in US$ terms), outperforming
major developed and emerging market indices, according to the Redseer Report.
3. Strong brand synonymous with trust, efficiency and transparency, across our trading platform as well as our
clearing, settlement and market supervisory role
• Our role as a first level regulator is operationalised through dedicated functions spanning investor protection, market
surveillance, issuer oversight and intermediary supervision.
• We work with Indian regulators such as SEBI and the International Financial Services Centres Authority (“IFSCA”)
on various policy matters, which further strengthens investor trust and confidence in capital markets.

2 In terms of number of new listings through initial public offerings (“IPOs”) for Fiscal 2026, according to the Redseer Report.

• We have built a reputation for efficiency by delivering low-latency, high-reliability trading infrastructure which has
processed 21.89 billion peak order messages in a day on March 24, 2026, on which date 201.00 million trades were
executed and on June 4, 2024, our platform processed a total of 293.85 million peak trades in a single day.
4. Track record of comprehensive and innovative offerings delivered through a vertically integrated business model
• In Fiscal 1995, NSE was the first stock exchange in India, among the ones still operational, to introduce a fully
automated, screen-based electronic trading system through the National Exchange for Automated Trading (“NEAT”)
platform, according to the Redseer Report. NSE Clearing Limited was India’s first clearing corporation to be
established and the first to provide a settlement guarantee mechanism, according to the Redseer Report.
• NSE Clearing Limited was one of the first clearing corporations globally to gradually transition to a T+1 settlement
cycle, further introducing a T+0 settlement cycle, strengthening the settlement mechanism, according to the Redseer
Report.
• Our focus on providing a seamless risk backstop to settlements is reflected in our Core SGF which was ₹130,791.51
million as of March 31, 2026.
5. Technology platform built for scale and resilience
• We have been designated as a CII by the NCIIPC. We have engineered an agile, robust and resilient infrastructure
with continuous investments in technology upgrades and security enhancements to ensure seamless operation of our
exchange platform.
• Our systems operate with combination of fault-tolerant servers (with inbuilt redundancy) and commodity servers, and
we maintain a 4:1 ratio for critical telecom links for persistent connectivity.
• We also have a strong cybersecurity track record and no data breaches of our operations in Fiscals 2026, 2025, and
2024.
• Our IT capital expenditure was ₹4,366.00 million in Fiscal 2024 and ₹4,220.26 million in Fiscal 2026 and our
technology expenses grew from ₹7,861.71 million in Fiscal 2024 to ₹13,145.75 million in Fiscal 2026.
• By deploying our existing systems with minimal modifications, we successfully launched NSEIX and commenced
live trading in June 2017. We upgraded the NSEIX systems within one and a half years and in July 2022, and
established NSEIX-SGX Connect at GIFT City which became fully operational in July 2023.
6. Combination of scale, growth, profitability and sustained cash generation
• Our Total income has grown to ₹187,133.70 million in Fiscal 2026 from ₹163,520.62 million in Fiscal 2024. Further,
in Fiscal 2026, we had one of the lowest non-volume-linked expenses, the highest adjusted operating EBITDA
margin, and one of the highest Profit After Tax Margin compared to leading listed stock exchange groups globally,
according to the Redseer Report.
• Further, our marginal cost of adding new products is low due to our scale.
• Our profitability is underpinned by consistent and sustained cash generation which allows us to self-fund investments,
maintain a high-quality capital buffer, and support ecosystem development.
7. Experienced and skilled management team committed to upholding strong corporate governance standards
• We have a dedicated and experienced management team with significant experience in the securities industry, client
service, regulatory supervision and the technology sector.
• As an MII, we place significant emphasis on maintaining robust corporate governance standards which ensure
transparency, accountability and integrity in our operations, thereby promoting trust among our stakeholders.
• We are guided by a robust framework that includes clear and regulatory-compliant organisational policies for risk
management, and compliance with regulatory requirements.
For further details, see “Our Business – Our Competitive Strengths” on page 186.

and (iv) Impact of new labour code and reduced by the sum of (i) Profit on sale of investment in associates, and (ii) Interest on income tax refund for the relevant period/year.
44. Normalised Profit Before Tax Margin from continuing operations represents Normalised Profit Before Tax from continuing operations divided by Normalised income for the applicable period/year, expressed as a
percentage for the relevant period/year. Normalised income is defined as the sum of (i) Total income, (ii) Share of profits of associates accounted for using equity method and reduced by Interest on Income tax
refund for the relevant period/year.

Total Revenue of Discontinued Operations and (v) Profit on sale of investment in subsidiaries classified in discontinued operations for the applicable period/year, expressed as a percentage, for the relevant
period/year.

The National Stock Exchange of India Limited (“NSE” or “the Parent Company” or “the Holding Company”)
established in 1992 is the first demutualized electronic exchange in India. NSE was the first exchange in the country
to provide a modern, fully automated screen-based electronic trading system which offered easy trading facility to
the investors spread across the country. NSE offers trading in equity, equity derivatives, debt, currency
derivatives and commodity derivatives segments.

Overview
We have been the largest stock exchange in India in terms of total turnover in cash market and total turnover in equity
derivatives (based on notional turnover for equity options) from Fiscal 20011 to Fiscal 2026, and we have been the largest stock
exchange in India in terms of total turnover in exchange-traded currency derivatives (based on notional turnover for currency

compared to the leading listed stock exchange groups globally, we were the largest multi-asset class exchange in terms of
number of trades in cash equities and contracts traded in equity derivatives in Fiscal 2026 with a global market share of 11.38%
in number of trades in cash equities and 51.18% in contracts traded in equity derivatives. We are a “first level regulator” in
India3, and in that role, are committed to providing equal, unrestricted, transparent and fair access to the stock market to all
market participants, including investors, issuers and intermediaries, while maintaining orderly and efficient market functioning
and safeguarding investor interests.
We operate a vertically integrated stock exchange - where we offer a simple, integrated platform for trading, clearing, listing
and other services such as data feed services, data terminal services and licensing services. We provide a comprehensive, one-
stop platform to manage regulatory compliance, risk monitoring, and post-trade settlement. We offer a diversified range of
products across multiple asset classes, including cash market, futures, options, mutual funds platform, commodity derivatives,
exchange-traded currency derivatives, wholesale debt market and interest rate futures, among others. Our operations are
supported by our proprietary technology infrastructure that is resilient and secure, supporting high-speed and high-frequency
transactions while ensuring seamless market operations, comprehensive market data dissemination, and allows for rapid
implementation of regulatory directives.

Regulatory Oversight and Governmental Policies
We operate in a highly regulated industry and are subject to extensive regulation. We are a “first level regulator” in India, and
in that role are committed to providing equal, unrestricted, transparent and fair access to the stock market to all market
participants, including investors, issuers and intermediaries, while maintaining orderly and efficient market functioning and
safeguarding investor interests. SEBI regulates us and has broad powers to approve or consent to proposals made by us, whether
with respect to rule amendments, product range or infrastructure or market development initiatives. SEBI may also conduct
periodic reviews, audits and inspections and issue suspension orders of our stock exchange. While regulation can constrain
certain activities, it also reinforces market integrity and investor confidence, which are foundational to sustained volume
growth. Below are some examples of key recent regulations introduced by SEBI and RBI that impacted our results of
operations:
• In January 2024, RBI issued revised directions governing exchange traded currency derivatives traded on stock
exchanges and clearing corporations. Under the updated framework, these entities shall not deal in or otherwise
undertake the business relating to foreign exchange derivatives unless they hold an authorisation issued by the RBI.
Stock exchanges are permitted to offer foreign exchange derivative contracts in specified currency pairs to both
resident and non-resident participants, with the RBI mandating that exchange-traded rupee derivatives be used only
for hedging purposes, alongside documentation and position limit requirements designed to ensure activity reflects
genuine exposure. In addition, where a participant’s open position exceeds US$100 million, the relevant stock
exchange must report day-end and intra-day peak position data to the designated authorised dealer or custodian. These
changes were one of the reasons for a decline in currency derivatives volumes.
• SEBI introduced a series of measures during Fiscal 2025 and Fiscal 2026 to strengthen the equity index derivatives
framework, implemented in phases. Among the most structurally significant were the rationalisation of weekly
expiries for index options, restricting each exchange to a single weekly expiry for one benchmark index effective
November 2024, and the standardisation of expiry days across exchanges, with our contracts moving to Tuesday
expiry effective September 2025. Additional measures included increasing the minimum contract size for index
derivatives, imposing additional margin requirements on short options contracts on expiry days, mandating upfront
collection of option premiums, tighter position limit monitoring, refined methodologies for measuring open interest
and effective exposures, enhanced intraday surveillance mechanisms and recalibration of risk management and margin
frameworks for index derivatives. These measures increased margin discipline, reduced the scope for concentrated or
leveraged short-term positioning, and aligned derivatives activity more closely with underlying cash market liquidity,
according to the Redseer Report. While intended to curb excessive speculation and protect retail investors, these
measures have moderated speculative turnover and contributed to a decline in trading volumes in equity futures and
equity options and related revenue in Fiscal 2026.
• Pursuant to SEBI’s circular dated October 1, 2024, clearing corporations with a clearing volume share of 40% or more
are required to maintain a minimum Core Settlement Guarantee Fund (“Core SGF”) corpus of ₹105,000 million for
equity derivatives products. This requirement reflects the introduction of additional stress testing scenarios for
determining the minimum Core SGF corpus. On March 23, 2023, the Governing Board approved a voluntary
contribution of 2% of transaction charges to the Core SGF. Accordingly, NSE Clearing Limited (“NCL”) augmented
the Core SGF corpus to the prescribed minimum of ₹105,000 million for equity derivatives products, achieving
compliance by December 31, 2024. Subsequently, in February 2025, our Governing Board approved the
discontinuation of our voluntary contribution of 2% of transaction charges to the Core SGF with effect from January
1, 2025, following the Core SGF having been adequately funded. Accordingly, during Fiscal 2026, we contributed
₹5.76 million to the Core SGF, as against ₹2,340.89 million contributed in the preceding Fiscal 2025. Additionally,
₹2,500.00 million earmarked from General Reserves for the Commodity Derivatives SGF in Fiscal 2019 was de-
allocated and reinstated during Fiscal 2024, pursuant to SEBI’s approval dated January 31, 2024.

Technology is fundamental to the operation of our business. We are India’s largest screen-based trading platform with market
leadership across asset classes, according to the Redseer Report. Our technology infrastructure processes an average of 12 to
14 billion messages daily, with 21.89 billion peak order messages processed in a single day and can also process ~5 million

Interest rates and funds available for investment
We earn income from investment and treasury activities. The funds available for investment are primarily derived from two
principal pools: (a) margin funds, comprising cash collaterals from clearing members and deposits received from trading
members; and (b) our own surplus funds. These funds are invested primarily in government securities, fixed deposits, mutual
funds (including overnight and liquid schemes of the highest credit quality) and corporate bonds, in accordance with our
investment policy and applicable SEBI prudential norms. On our balance sheet, the investments attributable to each of these
pools are reported under “Investments” (both non-current and current), other financial assets(non-current), cash and cash
equivalents, and “bank balances other than cash and cash equivalents”. The income earned on such investments depends
principally on (i) prevailing interest rates and market rates of return, and (ii) the quantum of funds available for investment
across each of the two pools described above, which are in turn influenced by the macroeconomic environment in India and
levels of market activity. The key characteristics of each pool are as follows:
- Margin funds. NCL requires its clearing members to deposit collateral for margin trading and settlement of trades. These
deposits are held by NCL at banks primarily as fixed deposits that can be redeemed at short notice. Under IndAS, since
the deposits are made with NCL, they appear on our Restated Consolidated Statement of Assets and Liabilities as bank
balances on the asset side, with a corresponding liability entry. The quantum of cash collateral available for investment is
determined by the margin policy applicable to the relevant trade, prevailing levels of market activity and open interest, and
the applicable settlement period. As trading volumes and open interest increase, the pool of margin funds available for
investment correspondingly expands, and vice versa. As of March 31, 2026, ₹301,466.62 million pertained to settlement
obligations and margin money from members compared to ₹158,798.86 million as of March 31, 2025 and ₹213,271.10
million as of March 31, 2024.
- Own surplus funds. Our profitability is underpinned by consistent and sustained cash generation, and we had no
outstanding loans or borrowings as of March 31, 2026. However, certain bank guarantees have been availed for our clearing
operations. We have an active treasury management function that invests our own surplus funds, generating investment
income which is classified as other income. This pool is influenced by our retained earnings, dividend distribution policy
and capital allocation decisions. We maintain a risk reserve by earmarking certain of our treasury investments on our
balance sheet, as determined by our Governing Board on an annual basis. We assessed reserve requirement towards
adequate risk capital management and transferred an excess amount of ₹37,280.00 million for the year ended March 31,
2026, from risk reserves to retained earnings within equity leading to a decrease in the Risk Reserve to ₹48,050.00 million
as of March 31, 2026 from ₹85,330.00 million as of March 31, 2025. As of March 31, 2026, the investments earmarked
towards the risk reserve amounted to ₹37,889.46 million within non-current investments, and ₹10,160.54 million within
current investments.
Key Components of Our Restated Consolidated Statement of Profit and Loss
Revenue from operations
Our revenue from operations comprises (i) revenue from contract with customers, and (ii) other operating revenues.
Revenue from contract with customers:
• Transaction charges: represents fees we earn from trading activity across our stock exchange (including NSEIX). We
generate transaction charges primarily from the cash market, futures and options. We also earn revenue from trading
activity through the mutual funds platform, commodity derivatives, exchange-traded currency derivatives, wholesale
debt market and interest rate futures. Transaction charges differ based on the type of product.
• Listing services: comprise listing fees, book building fees and processing fees, which are fees charged to issuers for
using our electronic bidding systems. Entities that list their securities on our Exchange (as well as NSEIX) pay one-
time initial listing fees, book building fees and processing fees at the time of listing. The initial listing fee is a
fixed amount that is reviewed periodically, while book building and processing fees are determined based on the size
of a company’s proposed securities offering. In addition, entities pay a recurring annual listing fee at the beginning
of each year that their securities remain listed on our stock exchange in an amount determined based on total paid-
up share capital, bond or debenture capital as well as market capitalisation of companies.

• Data Centre – Rack charges: are fees we receive from providing colocation data centre facilities to members of our
Exchange and NSEIX. Rentals as well as incidental charges collected from members for providing racks are also
classified under Data Centre - Rack charges.
• Data Connectivity charges: are the fees paid by market participants (such as brokers, institutional investors and high-
frequency traders) to our Exchange and NSEIX, to establish and maintain a physical or virtual link to connect and
transact on the exchange’s trading system with charges determined based on subscription to different categories of
Messages Per Second (MPS) per asset class.
• Data Feed & Terminal services: include income generated from our data feed and terminal business, providing trading
data (including real-time market data) sourced from our stock exchange through our online data feed service, data
subscription packages, and data terminal services fees. We operate this business through our Subsidiaries, NSE Data
& Analytics Limited and Cogencis Information Services Limited.
• Licensing services: comprises fees for licensing our Nifty Indices for launching products linked to Nifty Indices to
asset managers, to stock exchanges for introducing index linked derivatives contracts and other intermediaries such
as brokers, investors, etc. that monitor the equity capital markets and derive revenue from usage of indices.
We operate these indices through our Subsidiary, NSE Indices Limited.
• Clearing & Settlement Services: comprises revenue from Clearing & Settlement Services provided by our clearing
corporation to market participants. We provide our Clearing & Settlement Services through our Subsidiaries, NCL and
NSE IFSC Clearing Corporation Limited (“NSEICC”).
• Others: primarily includes our remaining revenue streams that are not directly attributable to the services mentioned
above, such as income from various ancillary services.
Other operating revenue:
Other operating revenue primarily includes income from investments that is generated from sources of funds related to our
operating activities. Income from investments primarily includes income that we derive from investing margin funds and cash
collaterals received from clearing members as well as deposits received from trading members. We invest these funds primarily
in government securities, corporate bonds, mutual funds and bank deposits. We follow our investments policy that is governed
by prudential norms of investment and the SEBI guidelines (wherever applicable) in investing these funds and we earn interest
income and income from redemption of units in mutual funds.

Financial Risk Management
Our business activities expose us to a variety of financial risks, namely liquidity risk, market risks and credit risk. Our risk
management policies are established to identify and analyse the risks faced by us, to set appropriate risk limits and controls and
to monitor risks and adherence to limits. Risk management policies and systems are reviewed regularly to reflect changes in
market conditions and our activities. Our senior management has the overall responsibility for developing and implementing
our risk management policies. We have constituted a Risk Management Committee to oversee the implementation of our risk
management policies. Our Risk Management Committee is supported by the Treasury Committee that provides assurance that
our financial risk activities are governed by appropriate policies and procedures and that financial risks are identified, measured
and managed in accordance with our policies and risk objectives. We have a dedicated Treasury department to ensure
investments are made as per the approved prudential norms of investment.
Management of liquidity risk
Liquidity risk is the risk that we face in meeting our obligations associated with our financial liabilities. Our approach to
managing liquidity is to ensure that we will have sufficient funds to meet our liabilities when due without incurring avoidable
costs. In doing this, management considers both normal and stressed conditions. A material and sustained shortfall in our cash
flow could impair investor confidence.
We maintain a cautious funding strategy, with a positive cash balance throughout the years ended March 31, 2026; March 31,
2025 and March 31, 2024. Cash flows from operating activities provides the funds to service the financing of financial liabilities
on a day-to-day basis.
Our treasury department regularly monitors the rolling forecasts to ensure we have sufficient cash on an on-going basis to meet
operational needs. Any short term surplus cash generated by the operations, over and above the amount required for working
capital management and other operational requirements, is retained as cash and cash equivalents (to the extent required) and
any excess is invested in interest bearing deposits and other marketable debt investments including the government securities,
mutual funds and exchange-traded funds with appropriate maturities to optimise the cash returns on investments while ensuring
sufficient liquidity to meet our liabilities.
Management of market risk

Business Combinations
The acquisition method of accounting is used to account for all business combinations, regardless of whether equity instruments
or other assets are acquired. The consideration transferred for the acquisition of a subsidiary comprises:
• the fair values of the assets transferred;
• liabilities incurred to the former owners of the acquired business;
• equity interests issued by us; and
• fair value of any asset or liability resulting from a contingent consideration arrangement.
Identifiable assets acquired and liabilities and contingent liabilities assumed in a business combination are, with limited
exceptions, measured initially at their fair values at the acquisition date. We recognise any non-controlling interest in the
acquired entity on an acquisition- by-acquisition basis either at fair value or at the non-controlling interest’s proportionate share
of the acquired entity’s net identifiable assets.
Acquisition-related costs are expensed as incurred. The excess of the purchase consideration, as given below, over the fair
value of the net identifiable assets acquired as on the date of acquisition, is recorded as goodwill;
• consideration transferred;
• amount of any non-controlling interest in the acquired entity, and
• acquisition-date fair value of any previous equity interest in the acquired entity
If the purchase consideration is less than the fair value of the net identifiable assets of the business acquired, the difference is
recognised in other comprehensive income and accumulated in equity as capital reserve provided there is clear evidence of the
underlying reasons for classifying the business combination as a bargain purchase. In other cases, the bargain purchase gain is
recognised directly in equity as capital reserve. Where settlement of any part of cash consideration is deferred, the amounts
payable in the future are discounted to their present value as at the date of exchange. The discount rate used is the entity’s
incremental borrowing rate, being the rate at which a similar borrowing could be obtained from an independent financier under
comparable terms and conditions. Contingent consideration is classified either as equity or a financial liability. Amounts
classified as a financial liability are subsequently remeasured to fair value with changes in fair value recognised in profit or
loss. If the business consideration is achieved in stages, the acquisition date carrying value of the acquirers previously held
equity interest in the acquiree is remeasured to fair value at the acquisition date. Any gains or losses arising from such
remeasurement are recognised in profit or loss or other comprehensive income, as appropriate.
Leases
Our lease asset classes primarily consist of leases for land, buildings and equipment. We assess whether a contract contains a
lease, at inception of the contract. Ind AS 116 defines a lease as a contract, or a part of a contract, that conveys the right to use

an asset (the underlying asset) for a period of time in exchange for consideration. To assess whether a contract conveys the
right to control the use of an identified asset, we assess whether: (i) the contract involves the use of an identified asset (ii) we
have substantially all of the economic benefits from use of the asset through the period of the lease and (iii) we have the right
to direct the use of the asset. At the date of commencement of the lease, we recognise a right-of-use asset and a corresponding
lease liability for all lease arrangements in which we are a lessee, except for leases with a term of twelve months or less (short
term leases) and low value leases. For these short-term and low value leases, we recognise the lease payments as an operating
expense on a straight-line basis over the term of the lease. The lease payments are discounted using the interest rate implicit in
the lease. If the rate cannot be readily determined, which is generally the case for our leases, the lessee’s incremental borrowing
rate is used, being the rate that the individual lessee would have to pay to borrow the funds necessary to obtain an asset of
similar value to the right-of-use asset in a similar economic environment with similar terms, security and conditions.
To determine the incremental borrowing rate, we:
• where possible, use recent third-party financing received by the individual lessee as a starting point, adjusted to reflect
changes in financing conditions since third-party financing was received.
• use a build-up approach that starts with a risk-free interest rate adjusted for credit risk for leases held by the Group,
which does not have recent third-party financing.
• make adjustments specific to the lease.
If a readily observable amortising loan rate is available to the individual lessee (through recent financing or market data) which
has a similar payment profile to the lease, we use that rate as a starting point to determine the incremental borrowing rate. The
lease liability is initially measured at amortised cost at the present value of the future lease payments. The lease payments are
discounted using the interest rate implicit in the lease or, if not readily determinable, using the incremental borrowing rates.
Right-of-use assets are generally depreciated over the shorter of the asset’s useful life and the lease term on a straight-line basis.
If we are reasonably certain to exercise a purchase option, the right-of-use asset is depreciated over the underlying asset’s useful
life. Refer note 1(ii)(f) for the other accounting policies relevant to leases.

Trade receivables are amounts due from customers for services performed in the ordinary course of business and reflect our

initially based on the transaction price as they do not contain significant financing components. We hold the trade receivables
with the objective of collecting the contractual cash flows and therefore measure them subsequently at amortised cost using the
effective interest method, less loss allowance for credit impairment.
